mainTopic: Vowing by a ספר תורה, and vows that forbid actions like sleeping
overview: A ברייתא teaches three rulings about a person who makes a נדר by a ספר תורה. A vow 'by the Torah' does nothing, a vow 'by what is written in it' works, and a vow 'by it and what is written in it' also works. The גמרא asks why the last ruling is needed, since it seems obvious. It gives three answers. רב נחמן says one case is a scroll on the ground and the other is a scroll held in the hand. The second answer is that both cases are on the ground, and the ברייתא uses the style of זו ואין צריך לומר זו. The third answer is that when he holds the scroll, even 'by it' alone counts as 'by what is written in it.' Then a new משנה teaches that a קונם vow forbidding sleeping, speaking, walking, or relations with one's wife is binding under לא יחל דברו. The גמרא then brings a מחלוקת between רב יהודה and רב נחמן about a vow 'sleep is forbidden today if I sleep tomorrow,' and notes that רב יהודה agrees in the reverse case.

steps.title: Three ways to vow by a Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives three rulings about vowing by a ספר תורה: 'by the Torah' does nothing, 'by what is written in it' works, and 'by it and what is written in it' works.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא: If someone makes a vow 'by the Torah,' he has said nothing. If he vows 'by what is written in it,' his words stand. If he vows 'by it and by what is written in it,' his words stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא with three rulings about making a נדר by a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scroll itself is just parchment and ink, so linking an item to it creates no vow. 'What is written in it' includes the names of ה׳, so that kind of vow works. The third ruling combines both and also works, and that third ruling is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes a vow (נדר)
He has said nothing, so the vow does not take effect
His words stand, so the vow takes effect
By what is written in it, which includes ה׳'s names

phrases.english: It is taught: One who vows by the Torah
phrases.notes: He means the physical ספר תורה, as in 'this item is to me like the Torah scroll.'

phrases.english: has not said anything.
By what is written in it, his words stand.

phrases.aramaic: בָּהּ וּבְמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בָּהּ — דְּבָרָיו קַיָּימִין.
phrases.english: By it and by what is written in it, his words stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion with the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow by the scroll alone does nothing. A vow by what is written in it, or by both the scroll and what is written in it, takes effect.

steps.title: Why teach the third case at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if 'what is written in it' alone already works, why does the ברייתא need to say that 'it and what is written in it' works?
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא teaches that 'by what is written in it' makes the vow stand. Then does it really need to tell us that 'by it and by what is written in it' also stands?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for including a ruling that seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If mentioning only 'what is written in it' is enough, then adding 'it' as well cannot make the vow weaker. So the third clause looks like it teaches nothing new. A ברייתא is not supposed to waste words.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches; the ברייתא states
Does it need to be said? In other words, isn't this obvious?

phrases.english: It teaches 'by what is written in it'
his words stand,
so 'by it and by what is written in it' — does that need to be said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the third clause of the ברייתא as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: The third clause of the ברייתא: 'by it and by what is written in it.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the smaller statement already works, the bigger one obviously works too, so there is no reason to teach it.

steps.title: רב נחמן: scroll on the ground versus scroll in his hand
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says the two clauses are about different situations. When the scroll lies on the ground, the person is thinking about the parchment, so he must say both. When he holds it, saying 'what is written in it' is enough because he is thinking about ה׳'s names.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: There is no difficulty. This case is when the Torah scroll is lying on the ground. That case is when he is holding it in his hand. When it lies on the ground, his mind is on the parchment. When he holds it in his hand, his mind is on the names of ה׳ written in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the question by saying the two clauses are talking about two different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the scroll is on the ground, we assume he is thinking about plain parchment, so 'what is written in it' alone is not enough; he must say 'it and what is written in it.' If he holds the scroll, his mind is on the אזכרות, so 'what is written in it' alone works. That means the third clause teaches something new after all.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
It is placed on the ground
He holds it in his hand
Parchment sheets, the plain material of the scroll
The names of ה׳ written in the scroll

steps.confusionAlert: The first 'הא' (this case) refers to the LAST clause of the ברייתא, 'it and what is written in it.' The second 'הא' refers to the middle clause, 'what is written in it.'

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: It is not difficult:
this is where the Torah scroll is placed on the ground,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the last clause, where he said both 'it' and 'what is written in it.'

phrases.english: that is where he holds it in his hand.
When it is placed on the ground, his mind is on the parchment.

phrases.aramaic: נָקֵט לַהּ בִּידֵיהּ — דַּעְתֵּיהּ עַל הָאַזְכָּרוֹת שֶׁבָּהּ.
phrases.english: When he holds it in his hand, his mind is on the names of ה׳ in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by separating the two clauses into different cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the two clauses into two different situations (אוקימתא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses describe the same situation, so the third clause adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: On the ground, he needs to say both 'it and what is written in it.' In his hand, 'what is written in it' alone is enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a vow depends on what the person is actually thinking about, and the setting tells us what that is.

steps.title: Second answer: both on the ground, using the style 'this, and certainly that'
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the whole ברייתא is about a scroll on the ground. The real news is that even then 'what is written in it' works. The third clause is added only in the style of זו ואין צריך לומר זו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say that the case is where the scroll is placed on the ground. This teaches us that even though it is on the ground, since he said 'by what is written in it,' the vow works. And the ברייתא teaches 'this, and there is no need to say that.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different answer: both clauses are about a scroll on the ground, and the third clause is just there as an obvious add-on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike רב נחמן's answer, here 'what is written in it' works even on the ground, because those words clearly point to ה׳'s names. The new idea is in the middle clause. The last clause adds nothing new; the ברייתא uses a known style of teaching a bigger point and then a more obvious one.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say; this brings a second answer
This is what it teaches us
It works; it is effective
'This, and there is no need to say that': teaching a new point and then an obvious one

steps.whatToRemember: So far there are two answers to why the ברייתא lists both clauses: (1) רב נחמן: different cases, on the ground versus in his hand. (2) Same case, on the ground, and the ברייתא uses the style זו ואין צריך לומר זו. The next step gives a third answer.
steps.confusionAlert: In this second answer, 'what is written in it' alone works even on the ground. That is the opposite of רב נחמן's answer, where on the ground he had to say both.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say: it is where it is placed on the ground.
And this is what it teaches us,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּמַחֲתָא עַל אַרְעָא —
phrases.english: that even though it is placed on the ground,
since he said 'by what is written in it,' it works.

phrases.aramaic: וְזוֹ וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר זוֹ קָתָנֵי.
phrases.english: And it teaches in the style 'this, and there is no need to say that.'
phrases.notes: The 'that' is the last clause, 'it and what is written in it,' which is obvious once the middle clause works.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the same קשיא from step 2, instead of רב נחמן's split into two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the extra clause as a teaching style (זו ואין צריך לומר זו), not a new ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Including an obvious clause means the ברייתא must be teaching something new with it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The new point is the middle clause: even on the ground, 'what is written in it' works. The last clause is added only as the obvious follow-up.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Either the clauses are different cases, or the ברייתא teaches the new point first and then adds the obvious one.

steps.title: Holding the scroll makes 'by it' mean 'by what is written in it'
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: the clause in question is about someone holding the ספר תורה. Since he holds it, saying just 'by it' is treated like saying 'by what is written in it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: that whole middle clause is about someone holding the scroll in his hand. The ברייתא is teaching that when he holds it, even if he only says 'by it,' it counts as if he said 'by what is written in it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more answer to the question from Step 2: why does the ברייתא need the clause 'it and what is written in it'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer says the clause is about holding the scroll, not about it lying on the ground. Because he is holding it, his mind is on the holy words. So even the short word 'by it' is read as 'by what is written in it,' and the vow works.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
The middle clause of a teaching
He is holding it in his hand
It is considered like / it is similar to

steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to why the ברייתא needs the clause 'it and what is written in it.' (1) It depends on whether the scroll is on the ground or held. (2) It is written in the style of זו ואין צריך לומר זו. (3) When the scroll is held, even 'by it' alone works.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
the entire middle clause too
is where he is holding it in his hand.
And this is what it teaches us:
since he is holding it in his hand,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא אָמַר אֶלָּא ״בָּהּ״
phrases.english: even though he only said 'by it,'
it is like one who said 'by what is written in it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third, alternative answer to the קשיא of Step 2, after the answers in Steps 3 and 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case of the clause (holding the scroll).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Saying just 'by it' should be like vowing by the parchment, which does nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: When he holds the scroll, 'by it' counts as 'by what is written in it,' so the vow works.

steps.title: Vows that forbid actions like sleeping or speaking are binding
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה teaches that a קונם vow forbidding sleeping, speaking, walking, or relations with one's wife is binding. Breaking it violates לא יחל דברו.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says: 'קונם that I sleep,' 'that I speak,' or 'that I walk,' or says to his wife 'קונם that I have relations with you,' then he falls under 'he shall not break his word.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists vows where a person forbids himself from doing an action, and it rules that these vows hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the vow is not about a food or an object. It is about an activity the person forbids on himself. The משנה says such a vow still counts, and breaking it violates the פסוק of לא יחל דברו.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין: our משנה
A vow word: 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'
I have marital relations with you
'He shall not break his word': the Torah's command to keep vows

phrases.english: MISHNA: 'Konam that I sleep,'
phrases.notes: He means: sleeping is forbidden to me like a קרבן.

phrases.english: 'that I speak,' 'that I walk,'
one who says to his wife
'Konam that I have relations with you'
he is under 'he shall not break his word.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה; the topic of vowing by a ספר תורה is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vows forbidding actions on oneself (sleep, speech, walking, relations) are binding under לא יחל דברו.

steps.title: רב יהודה: do not sleep today if sleeping tomorrow would make today forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The case is someone who vows that sleep is forbidden to his eyes today if he sleeps tomorrow. רב יהודה in the name of רב says he may not sleep today, in case he sleeps tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: if someone says 'sleep is קונם to my eyes today if I sleep tomorrow,' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: he should not sleep today, because maybe he will sleep tomorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a case about a vow on sleep with a condition. It gives the first opinion, the strict one of רב יהודה in the name of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Today's ban only becomes real if he sleeps tomorrow. If he sleeps today and then sleeps tomorrow, it turns out he broke the vow today. So רב worries he might sleep tomorrow and tells him to stay awake today.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא: the discussion on the משנה
Perhaps / lest: a worry about what might happen

steps.confusionAlert: Today is not forbidden yet. The worry is that sleeping tomorrow would look back and make today's sleep a broken vow.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was stated:
'Sleep is konam to my eyes today
if I sleep tomorrow,'
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
He should not sleep today,
lest he sleep tomorrow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the משנה's vow about sleep with a conditional case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a vow 'sleep is forbidden today if I sleep tomorrow,' he may not sleep today, out of concern he will sleep tomorrow.

steps.title: רב נחמן: he may sleep today without worry
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן disagrees. The person may sleep today, and we do not worry that he will sleep tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: he may sleep today, and we are not worried that maybe he will sleep tomorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the opposite opinion, the lenient one of רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right now nothing is forbidden. רב נחמן trusts the person to keep himself from sleeping tomorrow, so there is no reason to stop him today.

keyTerms.meaning: We are not concerned

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said: He may sleep today,
and we are not concerned that perhaps he will sleep tomorrow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The other side of the מחלוקת, disagreeing with Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He may sleep today; there is no concern he will sleep tomorrow.

steps.title: רב יהודה agrees in the reverse case
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה agrees with the lenient ruling when the vow is reversed: 'sleep is forbidden to my eyes tomorrow if I sleep today.' Then he may sleep today.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה agrees that if someone says 'sleep is קונם to my eyes tomorrow if I sleep today,' he may sleep today.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits רב יהודה's strict view. In the reverse case, even he says it is fine to sleep today.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case, sleeping today only makes tomorrow's sleep forbidden. Today's sleep can never become a broken vow after the fact. So there is nothing to worry about today, and even רב יהודה allows it.

keyTerms.meaning: And he agrees: a scholar admits a case where he does not argue

steps.whatToRemember: The question is whether tomorrow's act can make today's act forbidden after the fact. Only in that case does רב יהודה tell him not to sleep today.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda agrees regarding one who says
'Sleep is konam to my eyes tomorrow
if I sleep today,'
that he may sleep today.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the limit of רב יהודה's strict view from Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a vow 'sleep is forbidden tomorrow if I sleep today,' everyone agrees he may sleep today.
